northern-access.sourceSummary: Transport Canada describes air travel supporting northern essential services and year-round movement where road/seasonal shipping alternatives are limited.
northern-access.attributionLimits: Dated government account; original role perspectives below are constructed, not testimony on behalf of any named Indigenous community. No claim that every northern journey lacks alternatives.
northern-access.question: Use the account to explain a benefit of aviation for a remote community and a geographical/seasonal reason. Original roles are a resident needing time-sensitive access, an air-service operator facing cost constraints and an environmental planner. Compare what each prioritises; identify one cost or limitation and an alternative that would need checking.
northern-access.expectedEvidence: Connects the technology to an actual societal purpose, distinguishes urgent access from replaceable travel, and uses evidence rather than treating the three original roles as authentic quotations.
northern-access.nearMiss: All northern communities have identical needs and no other transport, or one efficiency proposal makes the cost and access problem disappear.
northern-access.changedCase: An original community now has a reliable all-season road and a nonurgent delivery. Explain what information would change the comparison rather than copy the original air-only conclusion.

humanitarian-access.sourceSummary: WFP describes UNHAS carrying humanitarian personnel and light cargo where crisis conditions restrict other suitable transport.
humanitarian-access.attributionLimits: Service-provider description, not proof every planned flight succeeds or an assessment of every humanitarian response. No disaster imagery or distressing role-play required.
humanitarian-access.question: Compare the stated UNHAS access problem with northern Canadian access. Describe what aviation can enable for responders and people receiving assistance, identify a remaining capacity/safety/cost constraint, and compare the perspective of a response coordinator with an original resident whose access is otherwise restricted.
humanitarian-access.expectedEvidence: Explains a concrete global societal contribution and a limit, compares common access needs with different causes, and avoids claiming flight alone resolves a crisis.
humanitarian-access.nearMiss: Air transport cures the underlying crisis, or every commercial flight has the same access necessity as a humanitarian service.
humanitarian-access.changedCase: An original safe surface route becomes available for bulky nonurgent freight. Explain why the best mode may now differ from urgent passenger/light-cargo access.

noise-and-climate.sourceSummary: The Canadian sources describe local aircraft noise and aviation greenhouse emissions alongside the benefits of transport. Operational/design choices can reduce some impacts without eliminating all harms.
noise-and-climate.attributionLimits: Qualitative evidence only. No decibel thresholds, emissions multipliers, legal restrictions or current progress claims are adopted; a target is not a measured achievement.
noise-and-climate.question: Prepare an evidence table separating local noise near an airport from wider climate consequences of emissions. Compare original perspectives of a nearby resident, a remote-service user and an operator. Assess quieter operations or fuel-saving/efficiency design against the relevant harm, then name what each fails to solve and what further evidence would judge the result.
noise-and-climate.expectedEvidence: Assesses environmental causes, affected groups, mitigation and remaining trade-offs instead of listing a plane or saying all flight is good/bad. Distinguishes less fuel per service from a guarantee of falling total emissions when flight numbers change.
noise-and-climate.nearMiss: Quieter means zero climate effect; a future target proves impacts have already vanished; or an efficiency improvement guarantees a decline in total emissions under any traffic level.
noise-and-climate.changedCase: An original fleet uses less fuel per flight but makes more flights. Explain why actual fuel/traffic evidence is needed for the total effect, while a quieter engine by itself does not establish a climate result.
